w:r.w:t: With the rapid development of marine resource exploration, underwater robotic operations, and marine ecological monitoring, Underwater Object Detection (UOD) has emerged as a research hotspot in the field of computer vision [1]. Unlike terrestrial environments, the underwater environment is characterized by extreme complexity and high uncertainty. Achieving high-precision and real-time UOD is not only significant for marine biodiversity conservation but also a core prerequisite for Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to perform complex tasks [2]. Although detectors based on Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), such as the YOLO series, have achieved remarkable success on terrestrial datasets, their performance often suffers drastic degradation when directly transferred to underwater environments. Distinct from visual perception in atmospheric environments, underwater optical imaging is severely affected by the medium itself, leading to prevalent issues such as color distortion, low contrast, and blurred details in underwater images [3]. These factors pose significant challenges to object detection algorithms. Specifically, these challenges mainly stem from three aspects: (1) Complex Underwater Optical Degradation: The selective absorption of light waves by water—where red light attenuates the fastest—leads to severe color casting (typically a bluish-green bias). Simultaneously, forward and backward scattering caused by suspended particles result in image blurring and hazing effects, severely masking the true features of targets [4]. (2) Morphological Diversity of Underwater Organisms: Many valuable underwater targets, such as sea cucumbers and starfish, belong to soft-bodied or invertebrate animals. Their body shapes are highly variable and lack fixed contours, making it difficult for traditional detection models based on fixed geometric priors to adapt [5]. (3) Small Scale and Dense Distribution: In real-world underwater scenarios, targets are usually small in size and densely distributed within the field of view [6]. During feature extraction, fine-grained texture information of small objects is prone to being lost during the
operations of CNNs, leading to severe missed detections [7].

To address the aforementioned challenges, existing research has primarily followed two technical paths: image enhancement-based preprocessing methods and deep learning-based end-to-end detection methods. However, both exhibit distinct limitations. The first category of methods aims to improve image quality from the source. Traditional methods perform reverse restoration based on physical models (e.g., the Jaffe-McGlamery model) [8], estimating the underwater degradation process by establishing light transmission equations. However, they rely on precise underwater optical parameters, which are difficult to obtain in practical applications, resulting in poor generalization. Data-driven methods represented by CNNs or Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can effectively improve visual quality; for instance,

[9] and UWCNN [10] achieved good color correction effects by training networks on large-scale synthetic data. However, they often suffer from domain shift issues, limiting their generalization ability on real underwater images. Recently, self-supervised and unsupervised methods have become research hotspots.

-GAN [11] and Water-Color Transfer [12] have attempted unpaired enhancement and color transfer techniques, respectively. However, such enhancement models are usually trained independently of downstream detection tasks. Their optimization objectives are often inconsistent with the discriminative features required by detectors, potentially even introducing artifacts that are harmful to detection [13].

The second category of methods focuses on enhancing the robustness of the detection model itself. Researchers have strengthened feature extraction capabilities by designing more powerful backbones, attention mechanisms, or multi-scale fusion strategies [14].
For example, LMFEN [15] proposed hierarchical deep convolutions to preserve fine-grained features during

[16] modified residual block structures to enhance the perception of blurred boundaries. Nevertheless, most works still employ standard convolution operations, where fixed sampling grids struggle to adapt to irregular and deformable target contours [17]. Meanwhile, to obtain a sufficiently large receptive field, models generally use
, which inevitably leads to the loss of semantic information for small objects, becoming a performance bottleneck [18].

In summary, the current field of underwater object detection faces a core contradiction: the two critical stages—image enhancement and object detection—are decoupled, lacking a unified framework guided by the improvement of final detection performance for collaborative optimization. Simultaneously, detection networks themselves possess inherent defects in handling target deformation and feature preservation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the overall framework and core modules of the proposed method; Section 4 presents experimental settings, result analysis, and discussion; Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

Underwater image enhancement and restoration aim to recover clear visual content from degraded observations. Their development has undergone a profound evolution from physical model-driven approaches to data-driven paradigms, and more recently, to task-driven strategies.

Physical Model-based Methods: The core of these methods lies in the mathematical modeling of the underwater optical imaging process. Beyond the widely used Jaffe-McGlamery model or its simplified forms, representative works such as Du et al. [19] proposed a method based on

theory to decouple illumination and reflectance components; Zhuang et al. [20] utilized physical absorption and scattering models to synergistically enhance contrast. Furthermore, various variants that achieve restoration by estimating background light and transmission maps [21] have also demonstrated clear physical interpretability. While these methods possess explicit physical meaning, their performance is highly dependent on the accuracy of parameter estimation, limiting their generalizability in complex and dynamic underwater environments.
Deep Learning-based Methods: With the rise of the data-driven paradigm, CNNs and

gradually become mainstream. UWCNN [10] utilized synthetic datasets to train enhancement networks, while Water-Net [9] and FDCE-Net [22] optimized visual quality through adversarial learning. However, most of these methods rely on synthetic data or carefully paired real-world data, whereas acquiring high-quality paired underwater images is extremely difficult. More importantly, these methods typically use pixel-level (e.g., PSNR, SSIM) or perceptual metrics as optimization objectives. Although the enhanced results are visually pleasing, they may suffer from a mismatch with the discriminative feature representation required by downstream high-level vision tasks (e.g., detection, segmentation) [13].

Task-Oriented Enhancement Methods: Recently, researchers have begun exploring task-oriented enhancement strategies. Approaches include jointly training the enhancement module with the task network [22] or introducing task-specific constraints into the loss function [23]. However, existing joint optimization frameworks often lack lightweight modeling of underwater color degradation mechanisms. Furthermore, most designs implement the enhancement module as a relatively complex sub-network, thereby increasing the overall model complexity and training difficulty.
2.2 Object Detection and Its Underwater Applications

Current mainstream detectors are categorized into two-stage (e.g., Faster R-CNN series) and one-stage (e.g., YOLO series, SSD) paradigms. Among them, the YOLO series, renowned for its excellent trade-off between accuracy and speed [24, 25], has become the preferred baseline model for computationally constrained platforms such as underwater robots. Additionally, Transformer architectures have been introduced into the detection field, such as DETR [26] and its variants, demonstrating powerful global modeling capabilities. However, their high computational cost limits their application in real-time underwater operations.

Addressing the challenges of the underwater environment, researchers have made multi-dimensional improvements to detection networks. These include designing multi-scale feature fusion structures to handle scale variations (e.g., S-FPN [27, 28]), introducing attention mechanisms to focus on blurred targets [29], and leveraging data augmentation to simulate degraded environments for improved robustness [30]. Nevertheless, most of these improvements are confined to the backend of the detection network. Regarding input image quality degradation, they typically
adopt an attitude of "offline pre-processing" or "passive adaptation," failing to achieve a deep coupling of enhancement and detection at the architectural level.
2.3 Network Design for Deformation Adaptation and Detail Preservation

The variable poses of non-rigid underwater organisms and the degradation of edges in tiny objects constitute two major difficulties in current detection tasks. Deformable Convolutional Networks (DCN) significantly enhance the capability to model complex geometric deformations by adding learnable offsets to each sampling point of the convolution kernel, allowing the receptive field to adaptively align with target structures [32]. The latest DCNv4 [31] has achieved further breakthroughs in computational efficiency. To address information loss during

, researchers have begun to utilize the multi-resolution characteristics of wavelet transforms to decompose and preserve high-frequency details in the frequency domain, as applied in super-resolution [33, 34] and
layers for object detection [35]. Such methods effectively prevent the edge textures of tiny objects from being completely obliterated during the feature map contraction process.

To rigorously benchmark the effectiveness of the "End-to-End Underwater Specialist" framework, we conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis against two categories of baseline methods:

Generic Object Detectors: Including the classic two-stage architectures (Faster R-CNN [cite], Cascade R-CNN [cite]) and the state-of-the-art one-stage YOLO series (YOLOv8 [cite], YOLOv10 [cite], YOLOv11 [cite], and the latest YOLOv12 [cite]).
Underwater-Specific Detectors: Including LEFEN [cite], DJI-Net [cite], ERL-Net [cite], Boosting R-CNN [cite], and GCC-Net [cite], which are specifically engineered for the underwater domain.
All comparative experiments were executed on the DUO and URPC datasets under identical training protocols and hardware configurations to ensure a fair evaluation.

Figure 6(a) illustrates the classification performance on the DUO dataset. The model exhibits exceptional performance for Starfish and Echinus, achieving recall rates of 0.91 and 0.90, respectively. The values in the off-diagonal cells between marine species are almost exclusively 0.00, indicating that the proposed method has successfully learned highly discriminative features, virtually eliminating inter-class confusion. This validates the effectiveness of the HWD module in preserving distinct frequency-domain texture features. The primary challenge lies in the Scallop class, which has a relatively lower recall of 0.66 and a significant miss rate (False Negative) of 0.34. This is attributed to the biological habit of scallops, which often bury themselves in sediment or camouflage against the seabed, combined with their small scale. Analyzing the last column, we observe that 59% of the false positive detections are misclassified as Echinus. This suggests that complex background textures in the DUO dataset share high morphological similarity with sea urchins, occasionally confusing the detector.

Figure 6(b) presents the results for the URPC dataset, which is characterized by higher turbidity. The model maintains high recall rates for Echinus (0.90), Starfish (0.85), and Scallop (0.81). Notably, the recall for Scallops on URPC is significantly higher than on DUO, suggesting that the

effectively enhances the contrast of scallops in turbid water, making them easier to distinguish. The lowest recall is observed for Holothurian at 0.72, with a miss rate of 0.28. Holothurians lack rigid geometric structures and exhibit soft, deformable bodies that blend seamlessly with the environment. While our
